passages.title: Section II: Reading Comprehension Part A - Text 1
passages.content:
The weather in Texas may have cooled since the recent extreme heat, but the temperature will be high at the State Board of Education meeting in Austin this month as officials debate how climate change is taught in Texas schools.

Pat Hardy, who sympathises with the views of the energy sector, is one of the members of the board who are pushing back against proposed guidelines that would emphasise the causes of climate change. "There are as many scientists working against all the panic of global climate change as there are those who are pushing it," she claims. "Texas is an energy state and we need to recognise that. You need to remember where your bread is buttered."

Most scientists and experts sharply dispute Hardy's views. Board members like her "casually dismiss the career work of scholars and scientists as just another misguided opinion," says Dan Quinn, senior communications strategist at the Texas Freedom Network, a non-profit group that monitors public education.

The debate in Texas, which will conclude with a vote on new science standards in November, comes at a time when schools across the country are facing growing calls to strengthen climate education. While a 2019 poll found that almost 80% of American parents and the wider public supported children being taught about climate change, the topic has become an ideological battleground, prompting school boards across the country to reject curricula that address climate change.

A 2020 study, published in the journal Nature Climate Change, gave US states a median grade of B-minus for how climate change was addressed in their public science standards. The authors found that public schools in 20 states had standards that failed to adequately acknowledge anthropogenic climate change, and that in six states, climate change was not mentioned at all.

Glenn Branch, deputy director of the National Center for Science Education, points out that state science standards serve only as a baseline for schools. Decisions on curriculum materials and what actually gets taught in the classroom are decentralized, leaving school boards and teachers to make their own choices. In Texas, as in many other states, climate education is typically integrated into Earth and space science, elective courses that are taken by a small proportion of high school students. It receives far less attention in subjects that are more widely taught, such as biology and chemistry. It is also less prominent in many social studies courses.

Branch points out that, even if a growing number of official guidelines and textbooks reflect scientific consensus on climate change, unofficial educational materials that convey more slanted perspectives are being distributed to teachers. They include materials sponsored by energy industry associations.

passages.title: Section II: Reading Comprehension Part A - Text 2
passages.content:
Communities throughout New England have been attempting to regulate short-term rentals, but they are running up against a powerful, well-funded industry that is seeking to preserve a system that is lucrative for investors and convenient for travellers.

Now, with home prices at record highs and historically low inventory across the country, some housing advocates blame short-term rentals for tightening housing stock and driving up housing costs. In some destination towns, businesses have had to close early or reduce hours because there is no affordable housing for their seasonal workers.

"We are at a crisis level on the supply of rental housing in our region," said Taylor Hall, the founder of an advocacy group that focuses on Cape Cod housing. "Without enough affordable housing, communities lose essential workers like teachers and municipal employees, and businesses and employers are having a hard time finding people to fill jobs."

However, short-term rentals also provide housing for tourists, pointed out Ryan Castle, CEO of a local association of realtors. "A lot of workers are dependent on tourists, and tourists need a place to stay," he said. Castle argued that towns shouldn't punish local property owners who are renting out a home to help pay their bills. "People are using the platform to make ends meet in a region where living costs are high."

In Massachusetts, a coalition of housing advocates and municipal leaders has filed a bill that would require short-term rentals to register with local governments and would give towns the authority to restrict or tax the properties. The bill would also establish a registry of short-term rentals to help communities keep track of how many units are operating.

Similar efforts have faced stiff opposition from the short-term rental industry. In Maine, short-term rental hosts have pushed back against local regulations, arguing they infringe on property rights and will hurt tourism.

Keith Horn, an urban planner who has studied the impact of short-term rentals, said short-term rentals themselves are not the issue, but developers who purchase multiple residential properties to run as mini-hotels are taking away long-term housing options.

"When you have individuals who are renting out an extra bedroom or their home for a couple of weekends a year to make some extra money, that's not what is causing the housing crisis," Horn said. "Issues arise when investors buy up homes strictly for short-term rentals to bypass regulations and taxes. Shouldn't they be treated and taxed like a commercial business?"

Horn said similar registration requirements could benefit struggling cities and towns across the region by giving them better data on how many properties are being pulled from the long-term housing market, but cautioned that regulation alone won't solve the underlying issue. "The real challenge is a persistent lack of housing supply across the board," he said.

passages.title: Section II: Reading Comprehension Part A - Text 3
passages.content:
If you're heading for your nearest branch of Waterstones, the biggest book retailer in the UK, looking for either Cormac McCarthy's The Passenger or Stella Maris, you might find it requires a bit of effort. The two novels are among the most anticipated books of the year, but in many Waterstones branches they are tucked away on a lower shelf or kept behind the cash register.

The reason is a credit dispute between Waterstones and Penguin Random House (PRH), the world's biggest trade publisher. Waterstones has reportedly put a cap on how much credit it will extend to PRH, meaning it has drastically cut back orders of the publisher's titles. The move is a response to credit limits PRH placed on the retailer during the pandemic.

Waterstones insists that it is not boycotting PRH books, but acknowledges that it has taken steps to manage stock levels. "We are committed to stocking PRH titles and supporting their authors, but we are also managing our stock prudently in response to the commercial terms offered to us," a spokesperson for the chain said. "As bookshops reopen and footfall returns, we hope normality will return to our trading arrangements."

The stand-off highlights the growing tensions between large publishing houses and high-street booksellers. While both need each other to thrive, the pandemic disrupted normal trading relationships and accelerated the shift to online purchasing. Bookstores were forced to close during lockdowns, leaving them saddled with unsold stock and delayed payments to publishers.

For authors, the dispute is a major headache. While big-name authors like McCarthy will still find buyers, lesser-known authors and debut novelists whose books rely heavily on browsing and staff recommendations could see their sales crushed. "It's the debut writers and mid-list authors who are really suffering," said literary agent Andrew Lownie. "They don't have the advertising budgets of established authors, and if their books aren't displayed prominently in the shops, readers simply won't discover them."

Lownie noted that the row comes amid a broader debate about diversity and consolidation in the publishing industry. "The publishing industry talks about diversity in terms of authors and staff, but it also needs a plurality of ways of delivering books to consumers," he said. "If one or two dominant players can dictate terms to everyone else, it makes the entire ecosystem much more fragile."

Smaller publishers, meanwhile, have quietly welcomed the extra space on Waterstones' shelves, seeing it as a rare opportunity to showcase their books to casual browsers.

passages.title: Section II: Reading Comprehension Part A - Text 4
passages.content:
Scientific papers are the record keepers of progress in research. Each paper builds on previous discoveries, using citations to credit earlier researchers. A citation is a vote of confidence, a nod to the shoulders of the giants on whose work a study stands. Citations help researchers trace how ideas develop over time, evaluate the validity of new findings, and determine which avenues of research are proving most fruitful.

Citations also carry high stakes: the careers of scientists and the reputations of their institutions hinge not just on how many papers they publish, but on the number of citations those papers attract. Funding agencies, tenure committees, and university rankings all rely heavily on citation metrics to measure academic productivity and influence.

This intense focus on citation counts has generated perverse incentives, giving rise to questionable citation practices. In recent years, a growing number of journals and authors have been accused of engaging in citation manipulation—an unethical practice where researchers or editors artificially inflate citations to game the system.

One common scheme involves "citation stacking," where a group of authors or journals agree to cite each other repeatedly to boost their metrics. Another involves predatory journals that accept almost any manuscript in exchange for publication fees, often requiring contributors to cite multiple papers from the journal's back catalog. In some cases, third-party companies known as paper mills offer "citation packages" for sale, allowing authors to buy citations to improve their academic standing.

Efforts to tackle citation manipulation have gained momentum as academic databases deploy advanced algorithms to detect suspicious patterns. Scopus, one of the largest scientific indexing services, has developed automated tools to flag unusual spikes in cross-citations among groups of journals. When irregularities are discovered, offending publications can be stripped of their impact factors or delisted entirely from the database.

However, experts say technology alone cannot solve the problem. As long as researchers face relentless "publish or perish" pressures and universities continue to use simple citation metrics to judge scholarly achievement, dishonest actors will find new ways to exploit the system. Reforming academic evaluation to emphasize quality and rigor over sheer numbers will be essential to restoring integrity to scientific research.

passages.title: Section II: Reading Comprehension Part B
passages.content:
[A] Last year marked the 150th anniversary of a series of Yellowstone photographs by the renowned landscape photographer William Henry Jackson. He captured the first-ever shots of iconic landmarks such as the Tetons, Old Faithful and the Colorado Rockies. Jackson snapped them on a late 19th-century expedition through the Yellowstone Basin that was conducted by the head of the U.S. Geological and Geographical Survey of the Territories, Ferdinand V. Hayden. The team included a meteorologist, a zoologist, a mineralogist, and an agricultural statistician.

[B] Two centuries ago, the idea of preserving nature, rather than exploiting it, was a novel one to many U.S. settlers. One of the turning points in public support for land conservation efforts—and recognizing the magnificence of the Yellowstone region in particular—came in the form of vivid photographs.

[C] As an effective Washington operator, Hayden sensed that he could capitalize on the expedition's stunning visuals. He asked Jackson to print out large copies and distributed them, along with reproductions of Moran's paintings, to each member of Congress. "The visualization, particularly those photographs, really hit home that this is something that has to be protected," says Alicia Murphy, Yellowstone's park historian.

[D] Throughout the trip, Jackson juggled multiple cameras and plate sizes using the collodion process that involved coating the plates with a chemical mixture, exposing them and developing the resulting images with a portable darkroom. The crude technique required educated guesses on exposure times, and involved heavy, awkward equipment—several men had to assist in its transportation. Despite these challenges, Jackson captured dozens of striking photos, ranging from majestic images like his now-famous snapshot of Old Faithful, to casual portraits of expedition members at the camp. While veterans of previous expeditions had written at length about stunning sights, these vivid photographs were another thing entirely.

[E] The journey officially began in Ogden, Utah, on June 8, 1871. Over nearly four months, dozens of men made their way on horseback into Montana and traversed along the Yellowstone River and around Yellowstone Lake. That fall, they concluded the survey in Fort Bridger, Wyoming.

[F] Though Native Americans (and later miners and fur trappers) had long recognized the area's riches, most Americans did not. That's why Hayden's expedition aimed to produce a fuller understanding of the Yellowstone River region, from its hot springs and waterfalls to its variety of flora and fauna. In addition to the entourage of scientists, the team also included artists: Painter Thomas Moran and photographer William Henry Jackson were charged with capturing this astounding natural beauty and sharing it with the world.

[G] The bill proved largely popular and sailed through Congress with large majorities in favor. In quick succession, the Senate and House passed legislation protecting Yellowstone in early 1872. That March, President Ulysses S. Grant signed an act into law that established Yellowstone as the world's first national park. While some locals opposed the designation, the decision was largely accepted—and Jackson's photos played a key role in the fight to protect the area. "I don't believe that the legal protection would have happened in the timeframe that it did without those images," says Hansen, journalist and author of Prophets and Moguls, Rangers and Rogues, Bison and Bears: 100 Years of the National Park Service.

[H] Perhaps most importantly, these images provided documentary evidence that later made its way to government officials. Weeks after completing the expedition, Hayden collected his team's observations into an extensive report aimed at convincing senators and representatives, along with colleagues at government agencies like the Department of the Interior, that Yellowstone ought to be preserved.

options.text: Last year marked the 150th anniversary of a series of Yellowstone photographs by the renowned landscape photographer William Henry Jackson. He captured the first-ever shots of iconic landmarks such as the Tetons, Old Faithful and the Colorado Rockies. Jackson snapped them on a late 19th-century expedition through the Yellowstone Basin that was conducted by the head of the U.S. Geological and Geographical Survey of the Territories, Ferdinand V. Hayden. The team included a meteorologist, a zoologist, a mineralogist, and an agricultural statistician.

options.text: As an effective Washington operator, Hayden sensed that he could capitalize on the expedition's stunning visuals. options.text: Throughout the trip, Jackson juggled multiple cameras and plate sizes using the collodion process that involved coating the plates with a chemical mixture, exposing them and developing the resulting images with a portable darkroom. The crude technique required educated guesses on exposure times, and involved heavy, awkward equipment—several men had to assist in its transportation. Despite these challenges, Jackson captured dozens of striking photos, ranging from majestic images like his now-famous snapshot of Old Faithful, to casual portraits of expedition members at the camp. While veterans of previous expeditions had written at length about stunning sights, these vivid photographs were another thing entirely.

options.text: Though Native Americans (and later miners and fur trappers) had long recognized the area's riches, most Americans did not. That's why Hayden's expedition aimed to produce a fuller understanding of the Yellowstone River region, from its hot springs and waterfalls to its variety of flora and fauna. options.text: The bill proved largely popular and sailed through Congress with large majorities in favor. In quick succession, the Senate and House passed legislation protecting Yellowstone in early 1872. That March, President Ulysses S. Grant signed an act into law that established Yellowstone as the world's first national park. While some locals opposed the designation, the decision was largely accepted—and Jackson's photos played a key role in the fight to protect the area. 'I don't believe that the legal protection would have happened in the timeframe that it did without those images,' says Hansen, journalist and author of Prophets and Moguls, Rangers and Rogues, Bison and Bears: 100 Years of the National Park Service.
